glossary.title: Word meaning
glossary.cell: The smallest unit of life. Fig's body is made of millions of cells.
glossary.tissue: A group of cells that work together, like muscle or skin.
glossary.nucleus: The part of a cell that holds the chromosomes.
glossary.dna: The molecule that holds the instructions for building and running a living thing.
glossary.chromosome: A long piece of DNA wound up tightly. Each chromosome carries many genes.
glossary.gene: A section of a chromosome that holds the instructions for one thing.
glossary.pair: Two chromosomes with the same genes: one from the mother, one from the father.
glossary.centromere: The pinched point where the two halves of a copied chromosome are joined.
glossary.copy: Before a cell divides, it makes a copy of each chromosome. The copy stays joined to the original.
glossary.version: Different forms of the same gene, like A and a.

vo.VO-A01.building: [proud] This [pause] is Fig. [pause, curious] Fig is an ember newt, and Fig [pause] is not impressed. [pause] She's about to have a very bad Tuesday.
vo.VO-A01.beginning: This is Fig. Fig is a newt.

vo.VO-A02.building: Herons are patient, elegant, [drawn out] and [deadpan] about as merciful as a pop quiz on a Monday. [pause] This one [pause] leaves with half of Fig's tail.
vo.VO-A02.beginning: A bird bites Fig. Fig loses half of her tail.

vo.VO-A03.building: Six weeks later, [pause, amazed] the tail's back. Bone, muscle, skin, even the stripes. [curious] Nobody sent Fig any instructions. [pause] [mysteriously] Or did they?
vo.VO-A03.beginning: Six weeks later, Fig has a new tail. How?

vo.VO-A04.building: [warm] Let's take a look inside. Fig's built from cells, and every one of them keeps a copy of the instructions tucked away in its nucleus.
vo.VO-A04.beginning: Fig's body is made of cells. Each cell has a nucleus. The nucleus holds the instructions.

vo.VO-A05.building: Those instructions are written in DNA, coiled up into chromosomes. [impressed] Stretch out the DNA from [drawn out] just one of your cells, and it'd reach about [pause] two meters. Coiled up, it fits somewhere you'd need a microscope to find.
vo.VO-A05.beginning: DNA is wound up into chromosomes.

vo.VO-A06.building: A gene is just a [emphasis] section of a chromosome. [pause] Think of a chromosome as a cookbook, and the genes are its recipes.
vo.VO-A06.beginning: A gene is a part of a chromosome.

vo.VO-A07.building: Chromosomes come in pairs: one from mom, [pause] one from dad. Within each set the same genes, but [curious] sometimes different versions. Our [emphasis] model newt has just [emphasis] two pairs. [amused] Real newts have a lot more. [deadpan] Ours [pause] is the budget edition.
vo.VO-A07.beginning: Chromosomes come in pairs. One comes from the mother. One comes from the father.

vo.VO-A08.building: Before a cell divides, it copies [emphasis]every single chromosome. The copy stays stuck to the original in the middle - that's where the famous X shape comes from. [pause] [kind but pointed] An X is one chromosome, [pause] copied. [curious emphasis] Not two.
vo.VO-A08.beginning: The cell copies each chromosome. The X shape is one chromosome and its copy.

vo.VO-A09.building: [encouraging] Your turn. One cell has to become two, and each new cell needs [emphasis]exactly what the old one had. [pause] No more, no less. [dry humor] Cells are very fussy about this.
vo.VO-A09.beginning: Make two cells. Each new cell needs all of the chromosomes.

vo.VO-A10.building: [kindly] That cell's missing a chromosome. [dry] It won't be building any tails. [encouraging] Try again.
vo.VO-A10.beginning: This cell is missing a chromosome. Try again.

vo.VO-A11.building: [pleased] Two cells, identical to each other [emphasis]and to the parent. [pause] [proud]That's mitosis: a copy machine with very high standards.
vo.VO-A11.beginning: Two cells. They are the same. This is mitosis.

vo.VO-A12.building: [curious and intriguied] At the stump, a [slight emphasis] little lump of cells starts to grow. They haven't yet decided what to be, but [subtle emphasis] every one of them has the full set of instructions. [pause] [curious] So [long pause]] how does one turn into bone, [pause] and another turn into skin?
vo.VO-A12.beginning: New cells grow. They all have the same DNA. Some become bone. Some become skin. How?

vo.VO-A13.building: [proud] Here's the trick. Every cell has every gene, but each one only uses some of them. Bone cells switch on the bone genes, and skin cells switch on the skin genes. [pause] Same cookbook, [pause] different recipes.
vo.VO-A13.beginning: Every cell has the same genes. Each kind of cell turns on different genes.

vo.VO-A14.building: [confiding] Okay, confession time: this model gets a few things wrong. Real cells don't wait around for you to drag anything, and real newts have way more chromosomes. [pause] But that's the point of a model. It's useful because it leaves things out.
vo.VO-A14.beginning: This model is simple. Real cells are different in some ways.

vo.VO-A15.building: Breeding season's next month, and Ada isn't worried. Every cell in Fig has the same DNA, so the paperwork should be easy... [pause] [dry humor, drawn out] Hold that thought.
vo.VO-A15.beginning: Next month, Fig will have babies. Remember: every cell in Fig has the same DNA.

vo.VO-A16.building: Mitosis gets all the attention, but it's actually the short part. A cell spends most of its life growing, working, and copying its DNA. That stretch is called [brief pause] interphase, [dry humor] and no, it is not a nap.
vo.VO-A16.beginning: Most of the time, a cell grows and copies its DNA. This is called interphase.

vo.VO-A17.building: Ada's taken a photo of a thin slice of Fig's new tail tip, frozen mid-growth. [curious] Every cell got caught at a different moment, kind of like a crowd photo at a school dance.
vo.VO-A17.beginning: This is a photo of cells from Fig's new tail. Each cell is at a different stage.

vo.VO-A18.building: [teacherly] Watch me sort the first three. Round nucleus, no chromosomes you can see? [pause] That's interphase. Chromosomes lined up across the middle? [pause] Metaphase. Two sets pulling apart? [pause] Anaphase.
vo.VO-A18.beginning: Look at this cell. The chromosomes are in a line in the middle. This is metaphase.

vo.VO-A19.building: [calmly excited] Now here's the clever part. If 3 out of 36 cells are in metaphase, then a cell spends about [pause, sound of a few presses on a calculator] one-twelfth of its cycle there. [pause] It's like that dance photo from earlier: if most people are huddled awkwardly together and, well, not dancing, then that's probably where most of the night went.
vo.VO-A19.beginning: More cells in a stage means the stage takes more time.

vo.VO-A20.building: Now let's look at Fig's old tail, the part the heron left alone. [surprised] Almost every cell's in interphase. [warm] These cells are done growing, and they've got jobs to do.
vo.VO-A20.beginning: In the old tail, most cells are not dividing. They have jobs.

vo.VO-A21.building: Same count, different organism. Noor's lunch onion has been sprouting roots in a jar on the windowsill, and root tips grow fast. [pause] [dry] The onion's also unimpressed.
vo.VO-A21.beginning: Now count cells from an onion root.

fb.recount.building: Count again. Touch each centromere (the dot) once for chromosomes. Then count every rod or half of an X for DNA molecules.
fb.recount.beginning: Count again. Count the dots. Then count the rods.

fb.pairsCountedAsOne.building: You counted pairs. A pair is two chromosomes, so count every rod or X on its own.
fb.pairsCountedAsOne.beginning: A pair is two chromosomes. Count each one.

fb.dnaDoublesAlways.building: These rods have not been copied yet. One single rod is one DNA molecule.
fb.dnaDoublesAlways.beginning: These are not copied. One rod is one DNA molecule.

fb.xIsTwoChromosomes.building: You counted each half of an X as a chromosome. An X is one chromosome, copied: count centromeres, not arms.
fb.xIsTwoChromosomes.beginning: One X is one chromosome. Count the dots.

fb.xIsOneDna.building: Each X holds two DNA molecules, one in each half. Count the halves.
fb.xIsOneDna.beginning: One X has two DNA molecules. Count each half.

fb.pairSameParent.building: Those two both came from the same parent. A pair is one from the mother (M) and one from the father (P).
fb.pairSameParent.beginning: A pair has one M and one P.

fb.pairByLook.building: Those two carry different genes: look at the length and the letters. Partners are the same length with the same gene letters, even if the versions differ (A and a).
fb.pairByLook.beginning: Partners are the same length. They have the same letters.

hint.pair1.building: Partners are the same length, have the same pattern of light bands, and carry the same genes (the same letter, capital or small).
hint.pair1.beginning: Find two that are the same length.

hint.pair2.building: Each pair has one M (solid paper) and one P (striped paper).
hint.pair2.beginning: Each pair has one M and one P.

hint.x1.building: An X is one chromosome that has been copied. It has one centromere.

hint.x2.building: Each X has two halves. Each half is one DNA molecule.
hint.x2.beginning: One X has two DNA molecules.

frame.count.building: There are ___ chromosomes because ___. There are ___ DNA molecules because ___.
frame.count.beginning: I count ___ chromosomes. I count ___ DNA molecules.

A1.R1.prompt.building: What is the smallest unit that is alive?
A1.R1.prompt.beginning: What is the smallest living part?

A1.R2.prompt.building: Name one part that plant cells have and animal cells do not.
A1.R2.prompt.beginning: Plant cells have a part that animal cells do not. Name it.

A1.R2.answer: A cell wall, chloroplasts, or a large central vacuole.

A1.R3.prompt.building: What does the cell membrane do?
A1.R3.prompt.beginning: What does the cell membrane do?

A1.R3.answer: It controls what goes into and out of the cell.

A1.R4.prompt.building: In the story, what grew back after the heron's attack?

A1.R4.answer: Fig's tail: bone, muscle, skin and even the stripes.
A1.zoom.title: Zoom into Fig

A1.zoom.body.building: Use the zoom buttons to go from Fig down to her DNA, one level at a time.
A1.zoom.body.beginning: Press Zoom in. Go inside Fig.

A1.zoom.fig.text.building: This is Fig. Her new tail is where we are going.

A1.zoom.tissue.text.building: A slice of tail: skin on the outside, muscle, and bone in the middle. Each layer is a tissue made of cells.
A1.zoom.tissue.text.beginning: The tail has skin, muscle and bone. They are made of cells.

A1.zoom.cell.text.building: One tail cell. The big round part in the middle is the nucleus.
A1.zoom.cell.text.beginning: This is one cell. The middle part is the nucleus.

A1.zoom.nucleus.text.building: Inside the nucleus are the chromosomes. Most of the time they are long, loose threads, tangled together. Our model newt has four.
A1.zoom.nucleus.text.beginning: The nucleus has chromosomes inside. They look like long threads.

A1.zoom.chromosome.text.building: One chromosome: a long piece of DNA. Before a cell divides, each thread coils up tight into a short, thick chromosome like this one.
A1.zoom.chromosome.text.beginning: This is one chromosome. It is DNA, wound up tight.

A1.zoom.gene.text.building: The highlighted band is one gene. One chromosome carries many genes.

A1.zoom.scale.cell: Real size: about 20 µm across (0.02 mm)
A1.zoom.scale.nucleus: Real size: about 6 µm across (0.006 mm)
A1.zoom.scale.chromosome: Real size: a few µm long when coiled up
A1.zoom.scale.gene: Not to scale: genes vary a lot in length

A1.zoom.dna.text.building: Unwind the chromosome and you find DNA: two long strands twisted round each other, joined by pairs that fit together like puzzle pieces.

A1.pairs.title: Chromosomes come in pairs

A1.pairs.body1.building: The two long chromosomes are one pair. The two short ones are the other pair. In each pair, M (solid paper) came from the mother and P (striped paper) came from the father.
A1.pairs.body1.beginning: Two long ones are a pair. Two short ones are a pair. M is from the mother. P is from the father.

A1.pairs.body2.building: Partners carry the same genes in the same places, and they share the same pattern of light bands. The letters show versions: A and a are two versions of the same gene.
A1.pairs.body2.beginning: Partners have the same genes. A and a are versions of one gene.

A1.copy.title: Copying makes the X

A1.copy.body1.building: Before a cell divides, it copies every chromosome. Step through the copying and watch the count strip.
A1.copy.body1.beginning: The cell copies each chromosome. Watch the numbers.

A1.copy.body2.building: The number of chromosomes stays at 4. The number of DNA molecules goes from 4 to 8.

A1.W1.prompt.building: Watch how to count chromosomes and DNA molecules in a cell that has copied its DNA.
A1.W1.prompt.beginning: Watch. Count chromosomes and DNA molecules.

A1.W1.step1.building: Find the centromeres: the dot where the two halves of each X are joined. Each centromere marks one chromosome.
A1.W1.step1.beginning: Find the dots. One dot is one chromosome.

A1.W1.step2.building: Count them: 1, 2, 3, 4. This cell has 4 chromosomes.

A1.W1.step3.building: Now count the halves of the Xs. Each half is one DNA molecule.
A1.W1.step3.beginning: Count the halves. One half is one DNA molecule.

A1.W1.step4.building: 4 chromosomes with 2 halves each make 8 DNA molecules.
A1.W1.step4.beginning: 4 times 2 is 8. There are 8 DNA molecules.

A1.G1.prompt.building: This cell has not copied its DNA yet. Count the chromosomes and the DNA molecules.
A1.G1.prompt.beginning: This cell is not copied. Count chromosomes. Count DNA molecules.

A1.G1.step1.building: Count the centromeres (the dots) to count chromosomes.

A1.G1.step2.building: Each single rod is one DNA molecule.
A1.G1.step2.beginning: One rod is one DNA molecule.

A1.G1.hint1.building: Each chromosome has one centromere (the dot).

A1.G1.hint2.building: A single rod has not been copied, so it is one DNA molecule.
A1.G1.hint2.beginning: One rod is one DNA molecule.

A1.G1.fb.correct.building: 4 chromosomes, 4 DNA molecules. Before copying, the two counts match.

A1.G2.prompt.building: Match each chromosome with its partner. Select one, then select its partner.
A1.G2.prompt.beginning: Find the pairs. Select one. Then select its partner.

A1.G2.step1.building: Look for two chromosomes that are the same length and carry the same gene letters.
A1.G2.step1.beginning: Find two that are the same length.

A1.G2.fb.correct.building: Both pairs matched: same genes, one from each parent.
A1.G2.fb.correct.beginning: Each pair has one M and one P.

A1.G3.prompt.building: These chromosomes have been copied. Count the chromosomes and the DNA molecules.
A1.G3.prompt.beginning: These are copied. Count chromosomes. Count DNA molecules.

A1.G3.step2.building: Count the halves of the Xs for DNA molecules.

A1.G3.fb.correct.building: 4 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules. Copying doubles the DNA, not the number of chromosomes.

A1.I1.prompt.building: Count the chromosomes and the DNA molecules in this cell.

A1.I1.fb.correct.building: 4 chromosomes and 8 DNA molecules, however they are turned.

A1.I1GF.prompt.building: A cell has 12 DNA molecules, and every chromosome in it is an X. How many chromosomes does it have?
A1.I1GF.prompt.beginning: A cell has 12 DNA molecules. All chromosomes are X shapes. How many chromosomes?

A1.I1GF.fb12.building: 12 is the number of DNA molecules. Each X holds 2 of them, so there are fewer chromosomes than that.

A1.I1GF.fb3.building: 3 is the number of pairs. Each pair is 2 chromosomes.

A1.I1GF.fb24.building: Copying doubles the DNA, not the chromosomes. Divide by 2 instead.

A1.I2.prompt.building: These chromosomes have been copied. Match each one with its partner.
A1.I2.prompt.beginning: These are copied. Find the pairs.

A1.I2.fb.correct.building: Matched. Copied or not, partners have the same genes and come from different parents.
A1.I2.fb.correct.beginning: Each pair has one M and one P.

A1.I3.prompt.building: Which of these is a gene?

A1.I3.hint1.building: Think back to the zoom: chromosome, then gene, then DNA.

A1.I3.fbChromosome.building: A chromosome holds many genes. A gene is only one section of it.

A1.I3.fbChromatid.building: Each half of an X is a whole DNA molecule with many genes on it.
A1.I3.fbChromatid.beginning: Half of an X has many genes.

A1.I3.fbSection.building: A gene is a section of a chromosome, like one recipe in a cookbook.
A1.I3.fbSection.beginning: A gene is a part of a chromosome.

A1.I3.fbCell.building: Cells hold chromosomes, and genes are sections of chromosomes.

A1.check.title: Checkpoint

A1.check.body.building: Three questions about cells from a different animal. Show what you know on your own: hints and worked steps are off.
A1.check.body.beginning: Three questions. Work on your own.

A1.C1.prompt.building: This cell comes from a different animal. Count its chromosomes and DNA molecules.
A1.C1.prompt.beginning: This is a different animal. Count chromosomes. Count DNA molecules.

A1.C2.prompt.building: Match the chromosomes from this animal into pairs.

A1.C3.prompt.building: What is true about the two chromosomes in a pair?
A1.C3.prompt.beginning: What is true about a pair?

A1.C3.optCopies: They are exact copies of each other.
A1.C3.optMother: Both of them come from the mother.
A1.C3.optSame: They carry the same genes, but versions can differ.

A1.C3.fbCopies.building: Exact copies are the two halves of an X. Partners come from two parents, so their versions can differ.

A1.C3.fbMother.building: One partner comes from the mother and one from the father.
A1.C3.fbMother.beginning: One is from the mother. One is from the father.

A1.C3.fbDifferent.building: Partners carry the same genes in the same places.

A1.C3.fbSame.building: Same genes, and the versions can differ (like A and a).
A1.C3.fbSame.beginning: Same genes. Versions can be different.

A1.end.title: Meet the chromosomes: done

A1.end.body1.building: Genes are sections of chromosomes. Chromosomes come in pairs, one from each parent.
A1.end.body1.beginning: Genes are on chromosomes. Chromosomes come in pairs.

A1.end.body2.building: An X is one chromosome, copied: 1 chromosome, 2 DNA molecules. Next: how does one cell become two?
A1.end.body2.beginning: An X is one chromosome with 2 DNA molecules.

A2.ui.left: {n} left in the parent cell. Select one.
A2.ui.pickCell: Now choose new cell 1 or new cell 2.

A2.ui.divided: Divided. Compare each new cell with the parent.

A2.R1.prompt.building: How many DNA molecules are in one X-shaped chromosome?
A2.R1.prompt.beginning: One X has how many DNA molecules?

A2.R1.answer: Two: one in each half of the X.

A2.R2.prompt.building: Where do the two chromosomes in a pair come from?
A2.R2.prompt.beginning: Where does each chromosome in a pair come from?

A2.R2.answer: One from the mother and one from the father.

A2.R4.prompt.building: Name one reason a living thing needs to make new cells.
A2.R4.prompt.beginning: Why does a body make new cells?

A2.R4.answer: To grow, to repair damage (like Fig's tail), or to replace old cells.
A2.intro.title: Your turn: copy a cell

A2.intro.body1.building: Fig's tail grows back because cells divide: one cell becomes two. Each new cell needs exactly what the parent cell had.
A2.intro.body1.beginning: One cell becomes two. Each new cell needs all the chromosomes.

A2.intro.body2.building: Next, try it your way. You can copy the chromosomes first, or not. Mistakes are fine: you will see what happens.
A2.intro.body2.beginning: Try it your way. Mistakes are OK.

A2.T1.prompt.building: Give each new cell everything the parent cell had. Select a chromosome, then a new cell. When the parent cell is empty, divide it.
A2.T1.prompt.beginning: Move the chromosomes into the new cells. Then divide.

A2.T1.fb.correct.building: Both new cells match the parent. How did you get there? Next, watch how real cells do it.
A2.T1.fb.correct.beginning: Both new cells match the parent.

A2.fb.missing.building: A new cell is missing a chromosome. Without copying first, there is only one of each chromosome to share, so one cell has to go without.
A2.fb.missing.beginning: A new cell is missing a chromosome. Copy first.

A2.fb.extra.building: A new cell has an extra chromosome, and the other is missing it. Both halves of one X went to the same cell: send one half to each.
A2.fb.extra.beginning: One cell got both halves of an X. Send one half to each cell.

A2.fb.mixed.building: The new cells don't match the parent: some chromosomes are doubled and some are missing. Each new cell needs one copy of every chromosome.
A2.fb.mixed.beginning: Each new cell needs one of every chromosome.

A2.mitosis.title: How a cell copies itself

A2.mitosis.body1.building: Step through and watch the count strip. First, every chromosome is copied: each one becomes an X, with two identical halves.
A2.mitosis.body1.beginning: First, the cell copies every chromosome.

A2.mitosis.body2.building: Then the Xs line up, and fibres pull the two halves of every X to opposite ends. One half of each X goes to each new cell.
A2.mitosis.body2.beginning: Then each X is pulled apart. One half goes to each new cell.

A2.mitosis.body3.building: That is why the copy comes first: without it, there would be only one of each chromosome to share. This whole process is called mitosis.
A2.mitosis.body3.beginning: This is called mitosis. The two new cells are the same as the parent.

A2.G1.prompt.building: Now divide this cell the way real cells do. Copy first, then send one half of each X to each new cell.
A2.G1.prompt.beginning: Copy first. Then send one half of each X to each cell.

A2.G1.step1.building: Press "Copy the chromosomes". Every chromosome becomes an X.

A2.G1.step2.building: Select an X and put it in new cell 1: one half goes there, and the other half stays to be placed.
A2.G1.step2.beginning: Put one half of the X in new cell 1.

A2.G1.step3.building: Put that other half in new cell 2. Do the same for every X, then divide.
A2.G1.step3.beginning: Put the other half in new cell 2.

A2.hint1.building: Copy before you divide: each new cell needs its own copy of every chromosome.

A2.hint2.building: Each X gives one half to each new cell. Never send both halves to the same cell.

A2.G1.fb.correct.building: Each new cell has one copy of every chromosome: the same information as the parent.
A2.G1.fb.correct.beginning: Both cells are the same as the parent.

A2.I1.prompt.building: This cell is from a different animal, with three pairs. Divide it so both new cells match the parent.
A2.I1.prompt.beginning: Divide this cell. Both new cells must match the parent.

A2.I1.fb.correct.building: Six chromosomes in each new cell, one copy of each, just like the parent.

A2.GF.prompt.building: A human skin cell has 46 chromosomes. It divides by mitosis. What do the two new cells have?
A2.GF.prompt.beginning: A skin cell has 46 chromosomes. It divides. What do the new cells have?

A2.GF.hint.building: Mitosis gives each new cell the same information as the parent.
A2.GF.hint.beginning: The new cells are the same as the parent.

A2.GF.opt46: 46 chromosomes each, the same as the parent

A2.GF.fb23.building: Halving happens when eggs and sperm are made, not in mitosis. Mitosis keeps the full set.

A2.GF.fb92.building: The copy is shared between the two cells, so the number does not double.
A2.GF.fb92.beginning: The copies are shared. Each cell gets 46.

A2.GF.fb46.building: Mitosis copies all 46, then shares them: each new cell gets the full set.
A2.GF.fb46.beginning: Each new cell has 46, the same as the parent.

A2.GF.fb46diff.building: Each half of an X is an exact copy, so both cells carry the same genes.

A2.I2.prompt.building: A cell divides. One new cell gets 3 chromosomes; the other gets 5. The parent had 4. What went wrong?
A2.I2.prompt.beginning: One new cell has 3. One has 5. What went wrong?

A2.I2.hint.building: 3 + 5 = 8: the cell did copy. Where did the halves of the Xs go?
A2.I2.hint.beginning: Look at where the halves went.

A2.I2.optNoCopy: The cell forgot to copy its chromosomes.
A2.I2.optBoth: Both halves of one X went into the same cell.
A2.I2.optExtraCopy: The cell copied one chromosome twice.
A2.I2.optNormal: Nothing; new cells are often different.

A2.I2.fbNoCopy.building: Without copying there would be only 4 chromosomes to share, not 8.

A2.I2.fbBoth.building: One X sent both halves to one cell: that cell got an extra, and the other is missing one.
A2.I2.fbBoth.beginning: Both halves went to one cell.

A2.I2.fbExtraCopy.building: Then there would be 9 halves, not 8. The count is right; the sharing went wrong.
A2.I2.fbExtraCopy.beginning: The count is 8. The sharing went wrong.

A2.I2.fbNormal.building: Mitosis makes two cells that match the parent. A cell missing a chromosome has a problem.
A2.I2.fbNormal.beginning: New cells should match the parent.

A2.check.title: Checkpoint

A2.check.body.building: Three questions about cells dividing. Show what you know on your own: hints and worked steps are off.
A2.check.body.beginning: Three questions. Work on your own.

A2.C1.prompt.building: Divide this cell from a different animal so both new cells match the parent.
A2.C1.prompt.beginning: Divide this cell. Both new cells must match the parent.

A2.C1.fb.correct.building: Both new cells match the parent.

A2.C2.prompt.building: After mitosis, how does the DNA in each new cell compare with the parent cell's DNA?
A2.C2.prompt.beginning: How is the DNA in the new cells?

A2.C2.optHalf: Each new cell has half of the parent's DNA.
A2.C2.optDiffer: The two new cells have different genes.
A2.C2.optDouble: Each new cell has twice as many chromosomes.
A2.C2.optSame: Each new cell has the same DNA as the parent.

A2.C2.fbHalf.building: Mitosis copies first, so each cell gets a full set.
A2.C2.fbHalf.beginning: Each cell gets a full set.

A2.C2.fbDiffer.building: The two halves of each X are exact copies, so both cells get the same genes.
A2.C2.fbDiffer.beginning: Both cells get the same genes.

A2.C2.fbDouble.building: The copies are shared out, one half to each cell, so the number stays the same.

A2.C2.fbSame.building: Same DNA, same chromosomes: two identical copies of the parent cell.

A2.C3.prompt.building: Before dividing, a cell has 6 chromosomes, and each one is an X. After mitosis, what does each new cell have?
A2.C3.prompt.beginning: A cell has 6 X-shaped chromosomes. It divides. What does each new cell have?

A2.C3.fb6and6.building: Each new cell gets one half of each X: 6 single chromosomes, 6 DNA molecules.

A2.C3.fb3and6.building: Mitosis does not halve the chromosomes: every new cell gets one of each of the 6.

A2.C3.fb6and12.building: The Xs are pulled apart, so the new cells get single halves, not whole Xs.

A2.C3.fb12and12.building: An X is one chromosome, copied. Its halves are shared between the two cells.

A2.end.title: Copy a cell: done

A2.end.body1.building: Mitosis copies every chromosome, then pulls the copies apart so each new cell gets one of each.
A2.end.body1.beginning: Mitosis copies, then shares. Each new cell gets one of every chromosome.

A2.end.body2.building: The two new cells have the same DNA as each other and as the parent. Next: how long does each part of this take?
A2.end.body2.beginning: The new cells have the same DNA as the parent.

mis.divideWithoutCopy: A cell can divide without copying first.
mis.bothHalvesOneCell: Both halves of an X can go to the same new cell.
mis.splitByParent: One new cell gets the mother's chromosomes and the other gets the father's.
mis.mitosisHalves: Mitosis halves the number of chromosomes.
mis.daughtersDiffer: The two new cells get different genes.
mis.daughtersKeepX: The new cells keep whole X-shaped chromosomes.
A2b.phase.interphase.look: Round nucleus; no chromosomes you can see.
A2b.phase.interphase.seen: a round, dark nucleus and no separate chromosomes
A2b.phase.prophase.look: Paler nucleus with short threads inside.
A2b.phase.prophase.seen: a pale nucleus with short dark threads inside
A2b.phase.metaphase.look: Chromosomes in a line across the middle.
A2b.phase.metaphase.seen: short dark chromosomes lined up across the middle
A2b.phase.anaphase.look: Two sets of chromosomes pulling apart.
A2b.phase.anaphase.seen: two groups of chromosomes moving to opposite ends
A2b.phase.telophase.look: Two new nuclei; the cell pinching in two.
A2b.phase.telophase.seen: a cell pinching in two, with a small nucleus at each end
A2b.cards.label: Reference cards
A2b.cards.pick: Choose a phase card, then click every cell that matches it.
A2b.cards.demo: Reference cards: these stay on screen the whole time.
A2b.tally.title: Your counts so far
A2b.tally.left: {n} cells in this step still to sort.
A2b.tally.done: Every cell in this step is sorted.

A2b.R1.prompt.building: What happens to every chromosome before a cell divides?
A2b.R1.prompt.beginning: What happens to chromosomes before a cell divides?

A2b.R1.answer: It is copied: each one becomes an X.

A2b.R2.prompt.building: After mitosis, how do the two new cells compare with the parent cell?
A2b.R2.prompt.beginning: How are the new cells and the parent the same?

A2b.R2.answer: They have the same chromosomes and the same DNA.

A2b.R4.prompt.building: What does the nucleus of a cell hold?

A2b.cycle.title: The cell cycle

A2b.cycle.body1.building: A dividing cell goes round and round a cycle. The slices show how much of the cycle each part takes: interphase is most of it.
A2b.cycle.body1.beginning: A cell grows, copies, and divides, again and again.

A2b.cycle.body2.building: The cycle is continuous: one part flows into the next. The five names are lines that scientists drew to talk about it; the cell does not stop between them.
A2b.cycle.body2.beginning: The parts flow into each other. The names help us talk about them.

A2b.slide.title: A slice of the new tail

A2b.slide.body.building: Each cell on the slide was caught at one moment of its cycle. If you count how many cells are in each part, you can work out how long each part takes.
A2b.slide.body.beginning: Each cell is at one stage. Count the cells in each stage.

A2b.W1.prompt.building: Watch the first three cells being sorted. The cards show what to look for.
A2b.W1.prompt.beginning: Watch. Sort the first three cells.

A2b.W1.step1.building: Cell 1: a round, dark nucleus and no chromosomes you can see. That is interphase.

A2b.W1.step2.building: Cell 2: chromosomes lined up across the middle. That is metaphase.
A2b.W1.step2.beginning: Cell 2: chromosomes in a line. Metaphase.

A2b.W1.step3.building: Cell 3: two sets of chromosomes pulling apart. That is anaphase.
A2b.W1.step3.beginning: Cell 3: two sets pulling apart. Anaphase.

A2b.G1.prompt.building: Now you sort the six cells in rings. Choose a card, click the cells that match, then check.
A2b.G1.prompt.beginning: Sort the six cells in rings. Then check.

A2b.I1.prompt.building: Sort the rest of the slide on your own. Then check: your counts go into the next step.
A2b.I1.prompt.beginning: Sort all the other cells. Then check.

A2b.hint.sort1.building: Look for a nucleus first. A round, dark nucleus with no threads: interphase. A paler nucleus with threads: prophase.

A2b.hint.sort2.building: No nucleus? Look at the chromosomes: one line in the middle is metaphase; two sets moving apart is anaphase; two new nuclei is telophase.
A2b.hint.sort2.beginning: One line: metaphase. Two sets: anaphase. Two nuclei: telophase.

A2b.fb.unsorted.building: {n} cells in this step are not sorted yet. Sort them all, then check.

A2b.fb.allRight.building: All {n} cells match the answer key.

A2b.T1.prompt.building: Use your counts. For each phase, work out its share of the cells (%), then its hours out of a {hours}-hour cycle.
A2b.T1.prompt.beginning: For each phase: what share of the cells? How many hours?

A2b.T1.step1.building: Example: if 3 of 36 cells are in metaphase, the share is 3 ÷ 36 = about 8%.

A2b.T1.step2.building: The share of cells is the share of time. 8% of 24 hours is 0.08 × 24 = about 2 hours.

A2b.T1.step3.building: Do the same for every phase. Your counts may differ from a classmate's: each slide is different.
A2b.T1.step3.beginning: Do the same for each phase.

A2b.hint.time1.building: Share of cells = cells in the phase ÷ all cells, × 100.
A2b.hint.time1.beginning: Cells in the phase ÷ all cells.

A2b.hint.time2.building: Hours = share × 24. Check: all the hours together should add up to about 24.

A2b.T1.fb.correct.building: Your table is right. Interphase takes most of the day; the parts of mitosis take an hour or two each.
A2b.T1.fb.correct.beginning: Right. Interphase takes the most time.

A2b.fb.percent-is-count.building: For {phase}, you wrote the number of cells, not their share. Divide {count} by {total}, then × 100.

A2b.fb.hours-is-percent.building: For {phase}, the hours are the same number as the percent. Hours are the share of {hours} hours, not of 100.

A2b.fb.hours-not-scaled.building: For {phase}, the share is right but the hours are not. Multiply the share (as a decimal) by {hours}.

A2b.fb.percent-not-of-total.building: For {phase}, check the share: {count} cells out of {total}, × 100.

A2b.I2.prompt.building: In your slide, which phase takes the longest? How do you know?

A2b.I2.hint.building: More cells caught in a phase means cells spend more time in it.

A2b.I2.optFewest: The phase with the fewest cells, because those cells finished fast
A2b.I2.optMost: The phase with the most cells, because cells spend longest there
A2b.I2.optSame: They all take the same time; the slide is random
A2b.I2.optResting: Interphase, because the cell is resting

A2b.I2.fbFewest.building: Few cells in a phase means cells pass through it quickly, so it is short.
A2b.I2.fbFewest.beginning: Few cells means a short phase.

A2b.I2.fbMost.building: A phase with more cells lasts longer: a cell is more likely to be caught in it.
A2b.I2.fbMost.beginning: More cells means a longer phase.

A2b.I2.fbSame.building: If every phase took the same time, the counts would be about equal. They are not.

A2b.I2.fbResting.building: Interphase is longest, but not because the cell rests: it grows and copies its DNA then.
A2b.I2.fbResting.beginning: In interphase, the cell copies its DNA.

A2b.GF.prompt.building: A chemical stops cells from moving past metaphase. After a few hours, what happens to the counts on a slide?
A2b.GF.prompt.beginning: A chemical stops cells at metaphase. What happens to the counts?

A2b.GF.hint.building: Cells keep arriving at metaphase, but none leave.
A2b.GF.hint.beginning: Cells arrive but do not leave.

A2b.GF.optPile: Metaphase cells pile up, and anaphase and telophase cells disappear
A2b.GF.optNone: Nothing changes; each phase is separate
A2b.GF.optSame: All five counts stay the same
A2b.GF.optInter: Interphase disappears, because metaphase is now faster

A2b.GF.fbPile.building: Cells flow into metaphase and get stuck, so they pile up there. Controlling when cells move on is how bodies control growth.

A2b.GF.fbNone.building: The phases are connected: blocking one backs up the cells behind it.

A2b.GF.fbSame.building: Cells still flow in, but none flow out, so the metaphase count grows.

A2b.GF.fbInter.building: Cells still leave interphase as usual; they just cannot get past metaphase.

A2b.O1.prompt.building: This slide comes from Fig's old tail. Sort every cell, then check.

A2b.O2.prompt.building: Almost every cell in the old tail is in interphase. Why?
A2b.O2.prompt.beginning: Why are most old-tail cells in interphase?

A2b.O2.hint.building: Compare with the new tail tip: which one is still growing?

A2b.O2.optDone: The old tail has finished growing, so few cells are dividing
A2b.O2.optDead: Cells in interphase are resting and not doing anything
A2b.O2.optFast: Interphase is very fast in old tissue
A2b.O2.optDiffDna: Old-tail cells have different DNA from new-tail cells

A2b.O2.fbDone.building: Finished tissue does its job instead of growing, so most cells stay in interphase. The growing tip has more dividing cells.
A2b.O2.fbDone.beginning: The old tail is done growing.

A2b.O2.fbDead.building: Interphase cells are busy: they do their jobs, and they grow and copy their DNA when they are getting ready to divide.

A2b.O2.fbFast.building: If interphase were fast, few cells would be caught in it. Almost all are.
A2b.O2.fbFast.beginning: Lots of cells means a long time.

A2b.O2.fbDiffDna.building: Every cell in Fig has the same DNA, made by mitosis.
A2b.O2.fbDiffDna.beginning: All the cells have the same DNA.

A2b.onion.title: Same count, different organism

A2b.onion.body.building: Onion root tips grow fast, like Fig's new tail. Count a slice of root tip the same way.
A2b.onion.body.beginning: Count cells from an onion root.

A2b.N1.prompt.building: Sort every cell in the onion root tip, then check.

A2b.N2.prompt.building: Using your onion counts and a {hours}-hour cycle, work out the share and the hours for interphase and metaphase.
A2b.N2.prompt.beginning: Work out the share and the hours.

A2b.N2.fb.correct.building: Right. The same method works for any growing tissue.

A2b.check.title: Checkpoint

A2b.check.body.building: Three questions about the cell cycle. Show what you know on your own: hints are off.
A2b.check.body.beginning: Three questions. Work on your own.

A2b.C1.prompt.building: In a slice of a growing leaf, 30 of 36 cells are in interphase. What does this tell you?
A2b.C1.prompt.beginning: 30 of 36 cells are in interphase. What does this mean?

A2b.C1.optRest: Most of these cells are resting and doing nothing
A2b.C1.optLong: Cells spend most of their cycle in interphase

A2b.C1.fbFast.building: More cells in a phase means a longer phase, not a faster one.

A2b.C1.fbRest.building: Interphase cells grow, work and copy their DNA.

A2b.C1.fbLong.building: Most cells are caught in interphase because it takes most of the cycle.
A2b.C1.fbLong.beginning: Interphase takes most of the time.

A2b.C1.fbBroken.building: 6 cells are dividing, so the leaf cells can divide.

A2b.C2.prompt.building: In a slice of root tip, 6 of 48 cells are in metaphase. The cycle takes 24 hours. About how long is metaphase?
A2b.C2.prompt.beginning: 6 of 48 cells are in metaphase. The cycle is 24 hours. How long is metaphase?

A2b.C2.fb6.building: 6 is the number of cells. 6 ÷ 48 is the share: one eighth.

A2b.C2.fb3.building: 6 ÷ 48 = one eighth, and one eighth of 24 hours is 3 hours.

A2b.C2.fb12.building: 12.5 is the percent. Hours are 12.5% of 24, not of 100.

A2b.C2.fb8.building: Check the share: 6 ÷ 48 is one eighth, so one eighth of 24 hours.

A2b.C3.prompt.building: On one slide, phase A has 9 cells and phase B has 2 cells. Which phase lasts longer?
A2b.C3.prompt.beginning: Phase A has 9 cells. Phase B has 2. Which is longer?

A2b.C3.optCannot: You cannot tell from a slide

A2b.C3.fbA.building: More cells caught in a phase means cells spend longer in it.

A2b.C3.fbB.building: Fewer cells means cells pass through quickly: phase B is shorter.

A2b.C3.fbSame.building: Equal times would give about equal counts.

A2b.C3.fbCannot.building: A slide is a snapshot of many cells at once, so the counts estimate the times.

A2b.end.title: Clock the cycle: done

A2b.end.body1.building: The cell cycle is continuous. Cells spend most of it in interphase, growing, working and copying their DNA; mitosis is the short part.
A2b.end.body1.beginning: Cells spend most of their time in interphase.

A2b.end.body2.building: Growing tissue has more dividing cells than finished tissue, and the share of cells in a phase estimates the share of time. Next: same DNA, different cells.
A2b.end.body2.beginning: Growing tissue has more dividing cells.

mis.phasesByShape: You can tell the phase from the cell's size or outline.
mis.moreCellsFaster: A phase with more cells is a faster phase.
mis.phasesEqual: Every phase takes the same amount of time.
mis.phasesSeparate: The phases are separate steps that don't affect each other.
mis.percentIsCount: The number of cells is the same as the share of cells.
mis.hoursIsPercent: The percent is the number of hours.
mis.hoursNotScaled: The hours don't depend on the length of the cycle.
mis.percentNotOfTotal: The share can be found without dividing by the total.

A2b.fb.look.interphase.building: {right} of {total} match the answer key. Look again at cell {n}: round nucleus; no chromosomes you can see means interphase.
A2b.fb.look.interphase.beginning: Look again at cell {n}. It is interphase.

A2b.fb.look.prophase.building: {right} of {total} match the answer key. Look again at cell {n}: paler nucleus with short threads inside means prophase.
A2b.fb.look.prophase.beginning: Look again at cell {n}. It is prophase.

A2b.fb.look.metaphase.building: {right} of {total} match the answer key. Look again at cell {n}: chromosomes in a line across the middle means metaphase.
A2b.fb.look.metaphase.beginning: Look again at cell {n}. It is metaphase.

A2b.fb.look.anaphase.building: {right} of {total} match the answer key. Look again at cell {n}: two sets of chromosomes pulling apart means anaphase.
A2b.fb.look.anaphase.beginning: Look again at cell {n}. It is anaphase.

A2b.fb.look.telophase.building: {right} of {total} match the answer key. Look again at cell {n}: two new nuclei; the cell pinching in two means telophase.
A2b.fb.look.telophase.beginning: Look again at cell {n}. It is telophase.

A3.ui.everyCell: Every cell in the lump has these chromosomes
A3.ui.sameDna: Same chromosomes in all three cells

A3.R1.prompt.building: In a slice of a growing tail tip, why are more cells dividing than in an old tail?
A3.R1.prompt.beginning: Why are more cells dividing in a growing tail?

A3.R1.answer: The tip is still growing; the old tail has finished growing.

A3.R2.prompt.building: After mitosis, how does the DNA in the two new cells compare with the parent?
A3.R2.prompt.beginning: How is the DNA in the new cells?

A3.R2.answer: It is the same: each new cell gets one copy of every chromosome.
A3.R3.answer: A section of a chromosome: one "recipe" in the cookbook.

A3.R4.prompt.building: Name two kinds of tissue in Fig's tail.
A3.R4.prompt.beginning: Name two tissues in Fig's tail.

A3.R4.answer: Any two of: skin, muscle, bone.
A3.stump.title: A lump of undecided cells

A3.stump.body1.building: At the stump, cells divide by mitosis and make a lump of new cells. Every one of them has exactly the same chromosomes.
A3.stump.body1.beginning: New cells grow at the stump. They all have the same chromosomes.

A3.stump.body2.building: Look at the count strip: same information as the parent. So how do some become bone and others skin?

A3.T1.prompt.building: Here is one cell from the lump. Try to make it into a bone cell. Switch genes on and off, then check.
A3.T1.prompt.beginning: Make a bone cell. Switch genes on or off. Then check.

A3.T1.fb.correct.building: A bone cell: only the bone gene is switched on. The chromosomes did not change at all.
A3.T1.fb.correct.beginning: Bone cell! Only the bone gene is on.

A3.fb.none.building: No genes are switched on, so the cell is still undecided. Switch on the gene for the kind of cell you want.

A3.fb.wrong.building: That gene makes a different kind of cell. Every cell has all three genes: choose which one to switch on.

A3.fb.extra.building: More than one gene is switched on, so the cell is mixed up. A finished cell uses only the genes for its own job.

A3.trick.title: Same cookbook, different pages

A3.trick.body1.building: Every cell in Fig has every gene. A bone cell switches on the bone gene; a muscle cell, the muscle gene; a skin cell, the skin gene.
A3.trick.body1.beginning: Every cell has the same genes. Each kind of cell turns on different genes.

A3.trick.body2.building: Look at the chromosomes under each cell: they are identical. Only the switched-on gene (glowing) is different.
A3.trick.body2.beginning: The chromosomes are the same. Only the glowing gene is different.

A3.G1.prompt.building: Make this cell into a muscle cell.

A3.G1.step1.building: Find the muscle gene and switch it on.

A3.G1.step2.building: Make sure the other genes are switched off, then check.

A3.hint1.building: Each kind of cell uses the gene for its own job.
A3.hint1.beginning: Use the gene for the job.

A3.hint2.building: Only one tissue gene should be on. Switching a gene does not add or remove any DNA.

A3.G1.fb.correct.building: A muscle cell: same chromosomes, with the muscle gene switched on.

A3.I1.prompt.building: Make this cell into a skin cell, with Fig's orange colour.

A3.I1.fb.correct.building: A skin cell. Three cell types so far, all from the same chromosomes.

A3.I2.prompt.building: Compare the DNA in one of Fig's skin cells and one of her bone cells.
A3.I2.prompt.beginning: How is the DNA in a skin cell and a bone cell?

A3.I2.hint.building: Both cells came from the same lump, by mitosis.
A3.I2.hint.beginning: Both came from the same cells.

A3.I2.optDiffDna: Different DNA: skin DNA and bone DNA
A3.I2.optSame: The same DNA, with different genes switched on
A3.I2.optLost: The skin cell lost its bone genes
A3.I2.optHalf: Each has half of Fig's DNA

A3.I2.fbDiffDna.building: Mitosis copies the DNA exactly, so every cell has the same DNA.
A3.I2.fbDiffDna.beginning: All cells have the same DNA.

A3.I2.fbSame.building: Same DNA in every cell; what differs is which genes are switched on.

A3.I2.fbLost.building: The bone gene is still there in a skin cell, just switched off.

A3.I2.fbHalf.building: Mitosis gives every cell a full set.
A3.I2.fbHalf.beginning: Every cell has a full set.

A3.GF.prompt.building: Does a muscle cell in Fig's tail still have the skin gene?
A3.GF.prompt.beginning: Does a muscle cell have the skin gene?

A3.GF.optGone: No, it was removed when the cell became muscle
A3.GF.optThere: Yes, but it is switched off
A3.GF.optOther: No, muscle cells have muscle DNA
A3.GF.optMutant: Only if the cell has a mutation

A3.GF.fbGone.building: Nothing is removed. The skin gene is still on the chromosome, switched off.

A3.GF.fbThere.building: Every cell keeps every gene. A muscle cell just doesn't use the skin gene.

A3.GF.fbOther.building: All of Fig's cells have the same DNA.
A3.GF.fbOther.beginning: All cells have the same DNA.

A3.GF.fbMutant.building: No mutation is needed: the gene is there in every cell.

A3.regrow.title: Rebuilding the tail

A3.regrow.body.building: Mitosis made enough cells; switching genes on made them bone, muscle and skin. Step through the regrowth again.
A3.regrow.body.beginning: Mitosis makes the cells. Genes make them different.

A3.P1.prompt.building: In the cold open, you predicted where Fig's body got the instructions to build a new tail. Read your prediction. What would you change or add now?
A3.P1.prompt.beginning: Read your idea. What do you know now?

frame.revise.building: Now I think the instructions came from ___, and the cells became different because ___.

bank.revise: DNA, chromosomes, genes, mitosis, switched on, same
A3.check.title: Checkpoint

A3.check.body.building: Three questions about how cells become different. Show what you know on your own: hints are off.
A3.check.body.beginning: Three questions. Work on your own.

A3.C1.prompt.building: A person's liver cell and nerve cell look and act very differently. Which is true about their genes?
A3.C1.prompt.beginning: A liver cell and a nerve cell. Which is true?

A3.C1.optLiverMore: The liver cell has extra genes the nerve cell does not
A3.C1.optSame: They have the same genes, but use different ones
A3.C1.optNoGenes: The nerve cell has no genes left

A3.C1.fbLiverMore.building: Every cell has the same genes; none gets extra.

A3.C1.fbDifferent.building: Cells in one body have the same DNA, made by mitosis.

A3.C1.fbSame.building: Same genes in both; each switches on the ones for its job.

A3.C1.fbNoGenes.building: Every cell keeps all its genes.

A3.C2.prompt.building: Make this cell into a skin cell.

A3.C2.fb.correct.building: Skin gene on, the others off.

A3.C3.prompt.building: Why is a muscle cell not a skin cell?
A3.C3.prompt.beginning: Why is a muscle cell not a skin cell?

A3.C3.optSwitched: It has the muscle gene switched on and the skin gene switched off
A3.C3.optMutation: A mutation turned its skin gene into a muscle gene
A3.C3.optFewer: It has fewer chromosomes than a skin cell
A3.C3.optParent: It came from a different parent cell with different DNA

A3.C3.fbSwitched.building: Same genes, different ones switched on.

A3.C3.fbMutation.building: No mutation is needed: both genes are in every cell.

A3.C3.fbFewer.building: Mitosis gives every cell the same chromosomes.

A3.C3.fbParent.building: All the cells came from the same lump, with the same DNA.

A3.end.title: Build a body: done

A3.end.body1.building: Every cell has the same DNA, copied by mitosis. Cells become bone, muscle or skin by switching on different genes.
A3.end.body1.beginning: Same DNA in every cell. Different genes are on.

A3.end.body2.building: That is how Fig rebuilt her tail. Next: where this model is wrong.
A3.end.body2.beginning: Next: what this model leaves out.

mis.undecidedIsDone: A cell with no tissue genes switched on is finished.
mis.genesAdded: A cell becomes a new type by gaining new genes.
mis.allGenesOn: A cell switches on all of its genes.
mis.differentDnaPerTissue: Each kind of tissue has its own DNA.
mis.genesLost: Cells lose the genes they don't use.
A4.limits.heading: Where this model is wrong
A4.limits.title: A confession

A4.limits.body1.building: Every model leaves things out. The card shows what ours simplifies, and what is really true.
A4.limits.body1.beginning: Our model is simple. Real cells are more complex.

A4.limits.body2.building: Leaving things out is what makes a model useful: it shows the main idea clearly. The trick is knowing what was left out.
A4.limits.body2.beginning: Models leave things out on purpose.

A4.R1.prompt.building: An X-shaped chromosome: how many chromosomes, and how many DNA molecules?
A4.R1.prompt.beginning: One X: how many chromosomes? How many DNA molecules?

A4.R2.answer: Two new cells with the same DNA as the parent.

A4.R3.prompt.building: Why do most cells on a slide look like they are in interphase?
A4.R3.prompt.beginning: Why are most cells in interphase?

A4.R3.answer: Cells spend most of their cycle in interphase, growing and copying their DNA.

A4.R4.prompt.building: How can a bone cell and a skin cell have the same DNA but be different?
A4.R4.prompt.beginning: How can cells with the same DNA be different?

A4.L1.prompt.building: Which is a real way our model newt is different from a real newt?
A4.L1.prompt.beginning: How is our model different from a real newt?

A4.L1.hint.building: Look at the first row of the card.

A4.L1.optMore: Real newts have many more chromosomes
A4.L1.optLabels: Real chromosomes are labelled M and P

A4.L1.fbMore.building: Our newt has 4 to keep the counting simple; real newts have many more.

A4.L1.fbNoCopy.building: Real cells copy their chromosomes before mitosis too; the model got that part right.

A4.L1.fbLabels.building: The labels are a model trick. Real chromosomes are not coloured or labelled.
A4.L1.fbLabels.beginning: Labels are only in the model.

A4.L1.fbHalf.building: Real mitosis keeps the full set, just like the model.

A4.L2.prompt.building: "Share of cells = share of time" only works if which is true?
A4.L2.prompt.beginning: When does "share of cells = share of time" work?

A4.L2.hint.building: Look at the timing row of the card.

A4.L2.optSame: Every phase takes the same time
A4.L2.optRandom: Cells divide at random, independent times
A4.L2.optFast: Phases with more cells are faster

A4.L2.fbSame.building: If phases took the same time, the counts would be equal; the method is for when they differ.

A4.L2.fbRandom.building: If cells were in step with each other, a slide would catch them all in one phase.
A4.L2.fbRandom.beginning: Cells must divide at different times.

A4.L2.fbFast.building: More cells means a longer phase, not a faster one.

A4.L2.fbRest.building: Interphase cells are busy, and that is not what makes the method work.

A4.check.title: Unit checkpoint

A4.check.body1.building: Five questions about new situations. Show what you know on your own: hints, worked steps and sentence starters are off.
A4.check.body1.beginning: Five questions. Work on your own.

A4.check.body2.building: Your first answer counts. The last question asks you to explain in your own words; your teacher will read it.

A4.C1.prompt.building: This cell comes from a sea star's arm, which is regrowing. Divide it so both new cells match the parent.
A4.C1.prompt.beginning: Divide this cell. Both new cells must match the parent.

A4.C1.fb.correct.building: Both new cells match the parent.

A4.C2.prompt.building: You cut your finger. New skin cells fill the cut. How does their DNA compare with the skin cells next to the cut?
A4.C2.prompt.beginning: New skin cells fill a cut. How is their DNA?

A4.C2.optHalf: They have half as much DNA
A4.C2.optNeighbour: The same DNA as the cells next to them
A4.C2.optNew: New genes for healing were added
A4.C2.optBlood: They copy DNA from the blood

A4.C2.fbHalf.building: Mitosis gives each new cell a full set.
A4.C2.fbHalf.beginning: Each cell gets a full set.

A4.C2.fbNeighbour.building: The new cells were made by mitosis, so they have the same DNA.

A4.C2.fbNew.building: No genes are added; healing uses the genes every cell already has.

A4.C2.fbBlood.building: Each new cell gets its DNA by mitosis from the cell that divided.

A4.C3.prompt.building: A plant's root cells and leaf cells look very different. Which is the best explanation?
A4.C3.prompt.beginning: Root cells and leaf cells look different. Why?

A4.C3.optLost: Root cells lost their leaf genes
A4.C3.optDiff: Roots and leaves have different DNA
A4.C3.optSwitched: They have the same genes, but different genes are switched on
A4.C3.optSun: Sunlight adds new genes to the leaves

A4.C3.fbLost.building: Root cells keep every gene; the leaf genes are switched off.

A4.C3.fbDiff.building: A plant's cells all have the same DNA, made by mitosis.

A4.C3.fbSwitched.building: Same genes everywhere; root and leaf cells switch on different ones.

A4.C3.fbSun.building: Light does not add genes; leaf cells use genes they already have.

A4.C4.prompt.building: Two skin slides: slide X, from a healing wound, has 14 of 36 cells dividing; slide Y, from healthy skin, has 2 of 36. Which came from the part that is growing faster?
A4.C4.prompt.beginning: Slide X has 14 dividing cells. Slide Y has 2. Which is growing faster?

A4.C4.optSame: Both are growing at the same rate

A4.C4.fbX.building: More dividing cells means more mitosis, so faster growth: healing tissue.

A4.C4.fbY.building: Fewer dividing cells means slower growth.

A4.C4.fbSame.building: The counts are very different, so the growth is too.

A4.C4.fbNeither.building: Skin cells divide all the time to replace old ones, faster in a wound.

A4.C5.prompt.building: In your own words: how can a body rebuild a lost part, like Fig's tail? Use the words mitosis, DNA and genes.
A4.C5.prompt.beginning: How does a body grow back a part? Use: mitosis, DNA, genes.

A4.end.title: Unit checkpoint: done

A4.end.body1.building: You used a model of chromosomes, mitosis and gene switches to explain how a body grows and repairs itself.
A4.end.body1.beginning: You used a model to explain growth and repair.

A4.end.body2.building: Models leave things out; knowing what they leave out is part of using them well.

A-end.title: Breeding season

A-end.body1.building: Mitosis builds and repairs Fig, and every cell it makes has the same DNA. The life cycle shows where that happens.
A-end.body1.beginning: Mitosis makes all of Fig's body cells. They have the same DNA.

A-end.body2.building: The grey half (making eggs and sperm, and fertilisation) is Part B. Something about it is going to surprise everyone.
A-end.body2.beginning: The grey part comes next, in Part B.

A-end.done.title: Part A: done

A-end.done.body1.building: Every cell in Fig's body has the same DNA: mitosis copies it faithfully, and genes switched on or off make bone, muscle and skin.
A-end.done.body1.beginning: Every cell in Fig has the same DNA.

A-end.done.body2.building: Hold that thought. In Part B, a DNA test says Fig is not the mother of her own hatchlings.
A-end.done.body2.beginning: In Part B: a surprise about Fig's babies.

mis.labelsAreReal: Real chromosomes come labelled and coloured.
A4.limits.chromosomes.model: Fig has 2 pairs of chromosomes (4 in all).
A4.limits.chromosomes.real: Real newts have many more: often a dozen pairs or more.
A4.limits.drag.model: You decide when a cell copies and divides.
A4.limits.drag.real: Real cells copy and divide on their own, controlled by the body.
A4.limits.labels.model: Chromosomes are coloured, striped and labelled M and P.
A4.limits.labels.real: Real chromosomes have no colours or labels; scientists stain them to see them.
A4.limits.timing.model: Share of cells = share of time.
A4.limits.timing.real: This only works if cells divide at random, independent times.
A4.limits.genes.model: Three genes, switched on or off.
A4.limits.genes.real: Real cells use thousands of genes, turned up and down in many steps.
A4.limits.cycle.real: A round number for the maths. Real cycle lengths vary by species and tissue.
